article.title: Lava Researchers Find 24,650 Exposed Server BMCs Leaking IPMI Password Hashes via 20-Year-Old Flaw
article.summary: Security firm Lava found 36,872 internet-exposed server BMCs; 24,650 leak password hashes through a 2004-era IPMI 2.0 flaw, CVE-2013-4786.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

More than 36,872 servers running IPMI management interfaces are reachable from the public internet, and 24,650 of them disclose password-derived authentication material to anyone who asks before login even completes, according to research from cybersecurity startup Lava reported by [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/24650-internet-exposed-bmcs-disclose.html) and [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/). The flaw is tracked as [CVE-2013-4786](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2013-4786), which the National Vulnerability Database describes as a defect in "the IPMI 2.0 specification" that "allows remote attackers to obtain password hashes and conduct offline password guessing attacks by obtaining the HMAC from a RAKP message 2 response from a BMC," with a CVSS base score of 7.5. [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/) notes the underlying protocol was "introduced in 2004," and describes the exposure as resting on "a 20-year-old vulnerability."

## What We Know

- **Scope of the exposure.** As of May 6, 2026, a scan of the public internet for IPMI services on UDP port 623 "uncovered 36,872 unique hosts," according to [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/24650-internet-exposed-bmcs-disclose.html). Of those, 24,650 disclosed the password-derived hashes before authentication finished.
- **Where the exposed hosts are.** [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/) reports that on a live exposure map it reviewed, the United States tops the list with 39% of the vulnerable servers. [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/24650-internet-exposed-bmcs-disclose.html) separately reports more than 14,000 of the exposed hosts are located in the U.S., with the rest concentrated in Germany, China, the Netherlands, and the U.K.
- **How weak the credentials are.** According to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/), 6,240 of the exposed hosts accepted an empty username during authentication and were also protected only by weak passwords, while 2,340 used administrator passwords that matched public dictionary wordlists.
- **Vendor-specific factory passwords.** Many of the exposed hosts are Supermicro servers still running the factory-issued password printed on the chassis label under the username "ADMIN," [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/) reports. [Lava's own report](https://lavahq.io/bmc) puts numbers on how fast those factory formats fall: benchmarked at 80 gigahashes per second, the Supermicro chassis-label password (10 characters, uppercase letters only) takes about 30 minutes to exhaustively crack, while HPE iLO's factory-sticker format (eight characters of uppercase letters and digits) takes about 35 seconds; truly random, rotated credentials, by contrast, resist offline cracking indefinitely, per the same report. Lava also lists well-known factory defaults — including "admin," "PASSW0RD," and Dell's iDRAC default "calvin" — that it says are recovered instantly from a wordlist with no brute-forcing required.
- **What a compromised BMC exposes.** A compromised BMC "gives attackers control of the entire server below the operating system," according to [Lava's report](https://lavahq.io/bmc), which warns that in data centers, "flat networks and reused credentials can turn one exposed interface into access to shared storage, critical systems, neighboring tenants, and potentially the entire cluster." [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/24650-internet-exposed-bmcs-disclose.html) reports that an attacker who compromises an exposed BMC can "sidestep traditional security controls, survive operating system reinstalls, and maintain access." [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/) adds that such access can let attackers "change low-level configurations, apply malicious firmware updates, and compromise the system at a layer not monitored by security solutions."
- **Vendor responses.** [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/) reports that Lava notified Supermicro in June; the company acknowledged the risk and said it would review its default password policy for future hardware, while pointing to existing guidance that recommends rotating default BMC passwords and isolating management networks. Lava also notified HPE but received only an automated response with no follow-up, the outlet reports. [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/24650-internet-exposed-bmcs-disclose.html) reports that Dell, asked separately about the underlying specification flaw, said "this is an inherent problem with the specification for IPMI v2.0" and that "there is no patch."
- **Who found it.** The research comes from Lava, described by [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/) as a "cybersecurity and infrastructure startup." [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/24650-internet-exposed-bmcs-disclose.html) names the researchers as Michael Katchinskiy and Yakir Kadkoda, identifying Kadkoda as "CTO and co-founder at Lava."
- **Recommended fixes.** Both outlets converge on the same baseline advice: keep IPMI and Redfish management interfaces off the public internet, rotate factory-issued BMC passwords during provisioning, restrict management-network access to dedicated private networks, and disable legacy IPMI authentication modes where possible, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/) and [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/24650-internet-exposed-bmcs-disclose.html).

## What We Don't Know

Neither outlet nor Lava's own report breaks down how many of the exposed hosts belong to cloud or GPU-hosting providers versus enterprise data centers, though [Lava's report](https://lavahq.io/bmc) separately warns the flaw can enable "AI blast radius" scenarios across shared GPU infrastructure. It is not publicly known whether any of the 24,650 exposed hosts have already been compromised in the wild, and HPE has not issued any public statement addressing the findings beyond the automated reply [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/) describes receiving on Lava's behalf.
